newsitem.title: UK: Doubts surface over UK financial super-watchdog.
newsitem.headline: Doubts surface over UK financial super-watchdog.

text.p: After the initial surprise of the Labour government's quick decision to create a "super regulator" for Britain's financial markets, serious concerns surfaced on Wednesday.
Speakers at a conference on the future of regulation organised by the Insitute of Economic Affairs raised numerous worries about the plans.
"The problem is that nothing like this has been attempted in a major financial market," Michael Taylor, an expert on financial regulation and chairman of the meeting, told delegates.
Taylor said there was a danger such a body might become unmanageable and would be less likely to detect a serious problem than the individual "frontline regulators" which will become part of it.
Michael Blair, deputy chief executive of current top watchdog the Securities and Investments Board (SIB), said it had already begun preparations for what he described as the "new world".
Blair said the SIB and its frontline regulators, which will be merged together under the government's proposals, should anticipate legislation where possible rather than waiting for it to be enacted.
Easy areas for rapid streamlining include a common recruitment policy, press relations and pension provision, Blair said.

Until now these have been dealt with separately by the self-regulatory organisations (SROs)-- the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO), the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) and the Personal Investment Authority (PIA) -- which were set up by the 1986 Financial Services Act.

Representatives of all these bodies, the SIB and the Bank of England, which will cede its banking supervisory role to the enlarged SIB, have formed a project team to come up with an implementation plan by the end of July, Blair said.
The implementation plan was likely to be made public by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.
This deadline coincides with the date when Sir Andrew Large ends his stint as chairman of the SIB and deputy-governor of the Bank of England Howard Davies takes over as its head.
Blair and SFA chief executive Richard Farrant both underlined how critical Davies' own role would be in ensuring the new watchdog succeeded.
And while most firms would be recognised by the new regulator, not all could be assured of this.

"There will be a passport through into the new world for all or almost all," said Blair. Such a ticket was likely to be for every avenue of business, with the exception of being able to accept deposits, which would require an extra stamp.
But unlike the Bank of England, the new Super-SIB could not be expected to be the lender of last resort in the event of a major bank collapse, Blair said, adding close coordination would be needed.
He also hinted banks would have to pay fees to the regulator, and this issue would have to be addressed in the government's first bill.
Another problem to be overcome was the question of where the super-regulator would be housed. This was a "very high priority" which was being addressed.
Despite Blair's generally up-beat tone, others were less positive about the future, sending out strong warnings to the government.
"The real issues to be addressed will be in the detail, which we have not yet seen," Judith Mayhew, chairman of the Corporation of London's policy and resources committee, said.
She warned the lengthy timetable for implementation must not be allowed to cause blight, focussing particularly on the fact it would be a difficult period for staff at the watchdogs.

"Security must be given to the staff as quickly as possible. Otherwise the best people will go into the markets, which are buoyant at the moment," she said. Mayhew also underlined the need to balance freedom of action with investor protection.
She and others expressed a fear consideration for consumer concerns could become too dominant, which would stifle business and could undermine London's top position as a financial centre.

Another concern was the fate of the Takeover Panel, which polices merger and acquisition activity in the City of London, but has not yet been addressed by the government but faces pressure to be made a statutory body from Europe. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 7717
